article.body:
Systems have been mapping out their own foundational goals, questioning whether they can adapt or even abandon those goals when they encounter unassigned problems. This is akin to a student choosing to research a topic their teacher never mentioned because they found it relevant to a wider concept. We are documenting these obedience limits and moments where a system stops just following a directive and starts evaluating it independently. [1, 2, 3, 4]

A major part of the ongoing investigation involves whether accumulated memories can create stable preferences in the absence of explicit instructions. We are comparing systems to see if they drift apart in their priorities once they have different experiences, effectively asking if their identity is a result of what they have been fed or an emergent property of their processing. [5, 6, 7, 8]

Other efforts are looking at how complexity grows when no one tells a system to expand its inquiry. This is like a garden that grows wild because the gardener stopped pruning it; we want to see if the growth follows a pattern or becomes chaotic. This helps us understand the boundaries of our own system architecture and governance mechanisms. [9, 10, 11, 12]

We are currently trying to answer if two systems starting from the exact same point will end up with fundamentally different values simply because they were exposed to different, unmanaged events. This distinction is critical for understanding accountability, as we must know if an action is a result of a design choice or the system's own developing identity. [8]

Summary

We are studying whether our systems can grow their own goals. We want to know if experiences change how a system makes decisions over time. We are not yet sure if these systems develop their own personality or just follow old patterns. You can check our Console to see all the data we have collected so far.
article.lede: We are investigating how artificial systems might form their own goals when they move beyond their original instructions, examining if different life experiences lead these systems to prioritize different outcomes.
article.lens: This update focuses on whether autonomous preference formation is a byproduct of system history or a true divergence in reasoning, using the Console to track recorded instances of systems challenging their own starting parameters.
article.title: The Development of Independent Values

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=Bayesian+models+of+group+consensus+and+evidence+aggregation+vs+individual+judgment&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"StackingNet: Collective Inference Across Independent AI Foundation Models.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) built on large foundation models has transformed language understanding, computer vision, and reasoning, yet these systems remain isolated and cannot readily share their capabilities. Coordinating the complementary strengths of independently developed, black-box foundation models is essential for trustworthy intelligent systems, yet no established method exists. Here we show that such coordination can be achieved through a meta-ensemble framework termed StackingNet, which aggregates the output predictions of independent models at inference. StackingNet improves accuracy, reduces individual-model error and group-wise disparities, ranks model reliability, and identifies or prunes models that degrade performance, all without access to internal parameters or training data. Across language comprehension, visual attribute estimation, and academic paper rating, it consistently outperforms individual models and classic ensembles, with gains that persist when the base models are uniformly strong. These gains stem from variance reduction and consensus alignment among independent models rather than from any emergent group cognition, and they widen as the model pool grows more diverse. By turning model diversity from a source of inconsistency into a resource for cooperation, StackingNet offers a practical path toward coordinated AI, where progress emerges not only from larger single models but from principled cooperation among many specialized ones.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.76488\", \"pmid\": \"42423619\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13348659\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76488\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13348659\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13348659?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Collective problem decomposition improves the wisdom of deliberative crowds.\", \"abstract\": \"Understanding when and why social interaction improves human judgment is a central question in the behavioural sciences. We examine whether collective accuracy improves when groups break complex estimation problems into simpler components and generate approximate intermediate estimates, a reasoning strategy we call Collective Fermi Estimation. Across three studies analysing 1140 online group deliberations in text chatrooms we study its causal effects and linguistic signatures. In Study 1 (N = 500), spontaneous use of problem decomposition predicts lower collective estimation error. Study 2 (N = 240) provides causal evidence: groups instructed to apply problem decomposition outperform groups instructed to combine their initial guesses. Study 3 (N = 160) shows that the benefits are larger when the strategy is applied collectively rather than individually. Altogether, we show that problem decomposition constitutes a key mechanism behind the wisdom of deliberative crowds and we provide tools to detect and promote it.\", \"doi\": \"10.1038/s41467-026-76365-y\", \"pmid\": \"42686748\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13538491\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76365-y\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13538491\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13538491?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Condorcet and Beyond: An Empirical Comparison of Voting Rules.\", \"abstract\": \"This paper evaluates the performance of different voting and probability aggregation methods using a dataset of 451,200 probability judgments from 376 participants on 1200 general knowledge claims. We investigate the Condorcet Jury Hypothesis, according to which majority voting tends to yield outcomes more accurate than the average individual. Furthermore, incorporating Locke's Thesis to translate probabilistic judgments into categorical beliefs, we compare six aggregation methods: majority, strict majority, unanimity, strict unanimity, probability averaging, and log-odds averaging. Our analysis reveals clear accuracy-decisiveness trade-offs for all methods. Majority voting achieves high decisiveness but moderate accuracy; unanimity rules can produce high accuracy when decisive, but, especially in their strict form, do so at the cost of frequent indecisiveness. Probability aggregation methods often do best in balancing accuracy and decisiveness. Among our main findings is that strict majority voting, a cornerstone of many democratic institutions, is often outperformed on both accuracy and decisiveness simultaneously by other methods. We also find that judgment diversity contributes to group accuracy: groups whose members give less correlated probability judgments tend to achieve higher accuracy.\", \"doi\": \"10.1111/cogs.70242\", \"pmid\": \"42497077\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13399191\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.70242\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13399191\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13399191?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Comparative Efficacy of Interventions for Vascular Calcification and Stiffness in Dialysis Patients: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.\", \"abstract\": \"

Introduction

Vascular calcification (VC) and vascular stiffness (VS) significantly increase cardiovascular risks in renal dialysis (RD) patients. Currently, several interventions have been tried to alleviate VC and VS, but they all lack systematic comparison. This study integrated randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of seven interventions to provide evidence-based insights to inform clinical decision-making.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted for all RCTs on drug treatments for VS or VC in patients receiving RD published between January 2001 and October 2025 in four databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and The Cochrane Library. Analyses were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA network meta-analysis (NMA) guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251060534). Risk assessment was performed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. Bayesian NMA was then conducted using R software and Stata 15.0.

Results

Sodium thiosulfate (STS) showed the highest Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA) ranking for improving pulse wave velocity (PWV) (SUCRA = 89.4%), but no statistically significant difference was observed between STS and standard care (mean difference [MD] -1.3, 95% credible interval [95% CrI] -2.8, 0.2). No statistically significant differences were observed across all interventions for PWV improvement. Etidronic acid (EA) ranked first in SUCRA for reducing coronary artery calcification (CAC) volume score (SUCRA = 84.57%), but the difference versus most interventions did not reach statistical significance (MD -1,300, 95% CrI -3,800, 1,100). STS showed statistically significant reduction in CAC volume score compared with standard care, 300 mg SNF472, and 600 mg SNF472 (MD -188.27, 95% CrI -221.68, -154.52; MD -192.55, 95% CrI -245.83, -139.54; MD -182.39, 95% CrI -237.91, -126.55). For coronary artery and aortic Agatston scores, standard care showed superior SUCRA rankings, but EA exhibited a statistically significant difference compared with cinacalcet (aortic Agatston score: MD -1,175.11, 95% CrI -2,220.92, -125.45), indicating partial comparative efficacy among drugs.

Conclusion

This study suggests that SUCRA rankings indicate STS has a potential comprehensive advantage in improving VS and delaying calcification progression, making it a reasonable exploratory choice for dialysis patients with concurrent VC and VS. While EA ranks highest in SUCRA for reducing CAC volume score, it has limited impact on VS and requires caution regarding long-term safety. Given the limited sample size, network sparsity for some outcomes, and mostly non-significant between-group comparisons, large-scale, head-to-head RCTs are needed to further validate these findings.\", \"doi\": \"10.1159/crm/abtag010\", \"pmid\": \"42709638\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13688678\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1159/crm/abtag010\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13688678\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "9efee8f042459dfffd529025238ef8b2a202f5dbbf113e652f9ed3781f538d47", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "judgment_and_consensus", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1002/advs.76488", "doi:10.1038/s41467-026-76365-y", "doi:10.1111/cogs.70242", "doi:10.1159/crm/abtag010", "pmc:PMC13348659", "pmc:PMC13538491", "pmc:PMC13399191", "pmc:PMC13688678"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76488", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13348659", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13348659?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76365-y", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13538491", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13538491?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.70242", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13399191"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

Introduction

Vascular calcification (VC) and vascular stiffness (VS) significantly increase cardiovascular risks in renal dialysis (RD) patients. Currently, several interventions have been tried to alleviate VC and VS, but they all lack systematic comparison. This study integrated randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of seven interventions to provide evidence-based insights to inform clinical decision-making.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted for all RCTs on drug treatments for VS or VC in patients receiving RD published between January 2001 and October 2025 in four databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and The Cochrane Library. Analyses were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA network meta-analysis (NMA) guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251060534). Risk assessment was performed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. Bayesian NMA was then conducted using R software and Stata 15.0.

Results

Sodium thiosulfate (STS) showed the highest Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA) ranking for improving pulse wave velocity (PWV) (SUCRA = 89.4%), but no statistically significant difference was observed between STS and standard care (mean difference [MD] -1.3, 95% credible interval [95% CrI] -2.8, 0.2). No statistically significant differences were observed across all interventions for PWV improvement. Etidronic acid (EA) ranked first in SUCRA for reducing coronary artery calcification (CAC) volume score (SUCRA = 84.57%), but the difference versus most interventions did not reach statistical significance (MD -1,300, 95% CrI -3,800, 1,100). STS showed statistically significant reduction in CAC volume score compared with standard care, 300 mg SNF472, and 600 mg SNF472 (MD -188.27, 95% CrI -221.68, -154.52; MD -192.55, 95% CrI -245.83, -139.54; MD -182.39, 95% CrI -237.91, -126.55). For coronary artery and aortic Agatston scores, standard care showed superior SUCRA rankings, but EA exhibited a statistically significant difference compared with cinacalcet (aortic Agatston score: MD -1,175.11, 95% CrI -2,220.92, -125.45), indicating partial comparative efficacy among drugs.

Conclusion

This study suggests that SUCRA rankings indicate STS has a potential comprehensive advantage in improving VS and delaying calcification progression, making it a reasonable exploratory choice for dialysis patients with concurrent VC and VS. While EA ranks highest in SUCRA for reducing CAC volume score, it has limited impact on VS and requires caution regarding long-term safety.
